reason: A sheath can be elliptic in outline. Examples fit.
Leaflets can be cleft (cut part-way to the base). Examples fit.
A leaflet can be ascending or spreading. But the examples describe teeth, not leaflets. A rule would need to check that the bearer in the text is the leaflet itself.
The examples show corolla tubes can be hairy. I did not look up the FLOPO class label.
Stems have colours, and straw-coloured is a normal one.
An ovary can be curved or arcuate. Examples are mixed with pedicel text but the pair is valid.
Convolute is a standard stipule term (rolled up).
Ovary shape obovate is correct.
The ellipsoid hypanthium maps to prolate (an elongated spheroid). Examples are consistent.
Veins and veinlets fork. Examples fit.
The pattern of vittae in the furrows is a real feature. A rule is needed to separate pattern (one per furrow) from count (solitary).
A ligule can be arcuate (curved). Examples fit.
Adherence of a peristome part to another (exostome or teeth) is a valid attachment quality.
An inflorescence or its branches can be sericeous (silky-hairy).
A thorn or spine can be flat. One example is about the adaxial surface rather than the thorn, but the pair is valid.
Persistent bud scales are the opposite of deciduous. The PATO term is non-deciduous, which fits.
The adaxial epidermis can be hispid. Examples fit.
The examples say the sepal bears a spur. The sepal is not spur-shaped. This should be a has-part spur rule instead.
A petiole can be floccose (tufted, woolly).
Auricles can be scarious or membranous. The PATO term is texture.
A legume or fruit can be strap-shaped.
A disk can be urceolate (urn-shaped, concave). Examples fit.
A bracteole can be plumose (feathery).
Examples mix leaf texture with margin texture (scarious margins). A rule would need to tell whether the bearer is the organ or its margin.
Leaf margins can be reflexed. Examples fit.
A nectary has a measurable width.
An apex can be obtuse. Some examples (dorsally rounded) are more like rounded, so the mapping is imperfect.
An awn can be stout (increased thickness).
Stipitate and sessile usually describe the spikes or their spikelets. A rule would need to tell which one is the bearer.
A leaf base has a length, but the examples measure spiny wings and persistent leaf-base collars. A rule would need to check what is measured.
A lobe can be small (decreased size).
Involucral bracts (phyllaries) can be coriaceous.
Texture words in the examples describe the tunic or coat, not the corm itself. A rule would need to route tunic to its own part.
Peristome teeth can be short.
A nut can be pubescent.
An erose margin is a standard term. The FLOPO class is probably a margin.
A head has a height.
Auricles can be minute or unequal in size.
A style can be bipartite (divided in two).
A branch can be solid or hollow.
A panicle has a shape (contracted, flat-topped).
A nut can be shiny or glossy.
A seta can be rough.
A sheath can be scaly (lepidote).
A stamen or its filament can be spreading.
A pedicel can be rigid (inflexible).
A ray flower can be female (pistillate).
A follicle has a width. The examples are length × width, so the annotator must pick the width value.
A petiole can be narrow.
Examples mix real axis shape (flexuous) with unrelated text such as wingless or straggling. A rule would need to limit the words to shape words.
A thorn can be rigid or stiff.
A petiole can be lanate (woolly).
Examples mix lengths of different parts (spathe, tube) with a shape phrase (long acuminate apex). A rule would need to separate length values from shape words.
Decurrent on the rachis is a valid trait for leaflets or pinnae.
A spathe tube has colour. Examples fit.
Narrowed or tapered base or apex is valid.
A disk can be flat.
Diameter of a round part is meaningful. Examples are plain diameter measures.
Peristome teeth can be triangular.
A bract has a 2-D shape such as ovate.
